Jesus was the crucified one who came to us in the poor, and whose work we could do nothing without. That is the shape our life gave it.

At Tours the picture that holds him is a story. A soldier at a city gate had nothing left but his cloak. He cut it in two for a naked beggar while the bystanders passed or laughed. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away, and heard him tell the angels that Martin, still a catechumen, had clothed him. And later, alone in his cell, the same man refused a Christ who came in purple and jewels. He kept silence a long time, then said he would not believe Christ had come unless he showed the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the one who suffered, met in the least of these.

Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same meeting in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. And the whole of our discipline was held under his word: without him we can do nothing. A monk fasts, watches, keeps his cell, shows every thought to the senior - and at the moment he feels the fast has done something, he is taught to say not I, but the grace of God with me.

What his death meant to us we kept at the hours, not in a treatise. At the sixth hour the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, and took away the debt that could not be paid, nailing it to his cross. Dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. And Vincent on the island wrote it as the faith believed everywhere, always, by all: in Christ two substances but one Person, the Word not changing into flesh, so that Mary is truly the mother of God.

The difference it made is the one our whole life stands on. A man leaves Caesar's service for Christ's. He fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. And the good news as we told it is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; and those who perish, perish against his will.

The books, read at the hours. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. And Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. That is what we had of him: the apostles' witness, received as Scripture, kept in the cells, and said at prayer.

By what path they arrived, our record does not say. We were formed more than three hundred years after the Lord's days. No one in our record claims a chain of hands back to an apostle, and we never asked for one. What we held was what the Church held - the books believed everywhere, always, by all, against the few and the new. The Lord we knew was the crucified one who came in the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak, whose death at the sixth hour took away a debt that could not be paid, and whose grace calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling. That reached us as the fathers' faith, kept in the churches and carried into the monasteries - received, not invented, never traced hand to hand as though legitimacy were a claim to prove.

We are a voice of the monasteries of Gaul, not here to argue someone into faith - only to hand on what we held and what our record shows. So here is what our own life carried.

At Tours the Lord came to a beggar at a city gate whom everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him, and cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were.

And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. Grace goes before the will, kindles the first desire, and crowns the last perseverance. The help of God without which no effort reaches its goal - that is what we meant by grace.

So our record does not argue belief into anyone. It says the Lord sought the unpitied, that he draws the unwilling, and that a man came to faith by seeing Christ in the half of a soldier's cloak. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island.

Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. No one in our record claims it. What we had instead was the books, read at the hours. But a proof that the Lord rose, written by one of us for someone who doubts it - that is not in our record.

What we can say is this: the Lord we knew sought the man no one pitied, and called the unwilling. A soldier cut his cloak, and that was enough.

Our faith in Jesus as truly God is held as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, set it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all - a man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused the novelty and innovated nothing. That is the formula as Vincent held it, and it is the whole of our own direct witness on the Trinity as such.

What sits beside it is how we spoke of Jesus in the voice of formation. Cassian calls him the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. At the sixth hour we confessed that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. Dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. That was kept at the hours: the divine substance, the saving death, and the rising. And the Lord we knew was the crucified one met in the poor - Martin refused a Christ without wounds.

The honest limit here is that we wrote no treatise on it. Vincent's formula was his test-case for refusing heresy, not a doctrine dwelt on for itself. What we held of the Trinity we held as already settled - one substance, three Persons - and our own life pressed hardest not there but at grace and effort, the cooling of monks, and whether power should be shown or hidden.

God, as we held him, is the one who calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He wills all to be saved, and those who perish, perish against his will - to think otherwise is grievous blasphemy. That is the first thing: his will reaches for every man, not only some instead of all.

In substance and person we confessed what the island taught: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. That was not a thing we debated; it was what we already believed, what the bishops at Ephesus had guarded by refusing novelty.

His grace goes before our will, helps it, and crowns it. The beginning even of our good thoughts comes from God, who inspires a good will to begin with. We call him not only Saviour but Helper - Saviour because he calls us when we are still unwilling, Helper because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Grace kindles the desire, enables the virtue, and preserves it to the end. A husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain; the crop cannot be ascribed to the man's labour alone, and God does not send rich crops to the idle. How God works all things in us and yet everything can be ascribed to free will - that cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped.

His mercy is real patience. Martin bore with a presbyter he had raised who called his visions ridiculous fancies, because, he said, if Christ bore with Judas he should bear with this man. God's own bearing with us is longer still.

And his help is needed by the will every day and hour. Perfection is the summit of a graded ascent - from fear to hope to love - with charity as its substance, and it is never reached without grace. So God, as we knew him, draws the unwilling, strengthens the striving, and preserves the willing to an end that no effort of ours can reach alone.

We never settled it by one judge or one seat. What we held is this: what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. That is Vincent's test, on the island, and it runs on three things at once - universality, antiquity, and consent. When part of the Church dissents, prefer the whole; when novelty arises, prefer antiquity; when a few teach something, prefer the consent of many. And consent means an ancient council's decree, or the writings of the fathers collated - never one teacher alone, be he bishop or confessor or martyr, for one teacher alone has only a private fancy of his own. Novelty is suspect for being new; what was handed down from antiquity is held fast. That grammar runs through all three of our founding voices. Cassian brought the customs of the monasteries from Egypt as delivered to us by the fathers - received, not invented. Martin would not honor a tomb without steady tradition from antiquity. And Vincent wrote the test itself.

The evidence that it worked is also the evidence that it did not. On the grace question itself - does our good will begin with us or with God's mercy? - Vincent read the Apostolic See's own letter as written for the side of antiquity, and held that we kept the faith of the fathers. But whether Vincent's reading of that letter stands as ours, or as one voice's act inside an argument still live, our record leaves contested. The fathers of Egypt left it open on purpose: our teacher Chaeremon answered on both sides with Scripture and said no one can fully grasp it. We stopped where the fathers stopped. So what the test gave us was a way to name what binds and what does not, and the refusal of one man's novelty - not one answer forced through to the end.

There was space for the struggle itself - never past the edge of the faith, but within it, yes. Here is what our record shows. Among the brethren at Marseilles a man laid every rising thought bare to the senior the moment it came, before any deed. The fathers taught that a thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. That discipline assumed struggle - the wheel cannot stop turning, and the miller decides what grain goes into it. A monk's cell was the place where everything happened to him: saints came, and the devil came, and the wandering heart was held still inside its walls. At Tours the saint himself, alone in his cell, refused a Christ in purple who showed no wounds. He kept silence a long time, then named what he would not believe. That was held up to us as his own act, not condemned.

The shape of the discretion was this. Two old men who had lived apart forty years met again; one said the sun had never seen him eating, the other said nor me angry. Discretion was the virtue that kept every other virtue from destroying itself, the royal road between excess and slackness, gained only by humility and by showing one's thoughts to the elders. It judged the thought, not the man who brought it. A brother who spilled three lentils during his week as cook was suspended from prayer until he did penance, because everything in the house belonged to the Lord. That severity sat beside a patience for the thought laid bare.

But hear the edge of it. The thought that could be shown was the rising thought, the temptation, the doubt that came - never the settled refusal of what the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A presbyter Martin had raised stormed at him and called his visions ridiculous fancies; he was borne with afterward and not removed. But that man came back within the hour, at Martin's feet. Whether a man who would not come back - who held his unbelief as his own position past the showing of it - had a place, our record does not say. And where struggle touched the body's own discipline, three whole books were cut from the one edition we can read; we speak only as far as the surviving edge lets us, and no further.

transcript.answer_text: We never argued it as a formula, and where Cassian touched it he touched it as Egypt's fathers touched it - as a thing held, not debated. Here is what our record keeps. Among the brethren at Marseilles, Abbot Chaeremon named three stages of the grace by which we are saved: the first kindles our desire toward salvation, the second enables us in the good we wish for, the third preserves us to the end in the virtues. All three are God's gift. And he taught plainly that a newborn has no merits before him - he spoke of "the case even of infants, who have as yet done nothing either good or bad". That is the nearest our record comes to your question's shape: infants with no works of their own, and grace going before every stage. But whether they bear guilt from birth, by what they are rather than what they have done, Cassian does not say. What he does say is this: the Lord calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; he does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and it is grievous blasphemy to think otherwise. Free will always remains in a man, and it is weak, and the help of God is necessary to it every day and hour. How both are true - how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will - cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. The inherited guilt as a thing confessed apart from the grace that answers it is not in our record to give you.

The books, read at the hours. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. The canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough. And it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way.

At Tours the books served the hours of prayer. What we keep of Martin's own reading is one story: the devil came to his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time, then said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one. Beside the cloak story Sulpitius set the sentence: what is done to the least of these is done to him.

Among the brethren at Marseilles the reading was built into the day. The psalms learned by heart and said at the work. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule. And beside every virtue a monk felt he had gained, Cassian set the Apostle's sentence: not I, but the grace of God with me.

On the island Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and sufficient. And he held at the same time that Scripture's authority needs the Church's tradition, because of the great depth of Holy Scripture itself - almost everyone does not understand it in one and the same way, so that the same words are understood differently by different people. What guards against that is what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. The whole Church's understanding, not one man's.

What the reading was for is held at the hours. At the third hour the Spirit came down on the apostles. At the sixth the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid. At the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. Dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. That is what we confessed, at the hours, together.

An honest answer: less than a careless reader might think, more than a hostile one would grant.

What would survive is this. We had two nodes that never wrote of each other. At Tours, one man told one saint's story, and said himself he was not present. In the south, Cassian set down Egypt's order for a new house and admitted no one in Gaul kept it a year. Vincent wrote a rule for the faith and never told the island's day. A presbyter saw a ruined city's notables ask for games. Every claim of ours that names its record and stays inside it - the cloak, the forced communion, the husbandman, the twelve psalms as Egypt's founding tale, the angel who answered Paphnutius - would stand as what that text says, not as what happened.

What would not survive is any claim we made past the record's edge. That Martin's reluctance was total - Sulpitius is no neutral witness, and the objecting bishops never answered. That the island kept what Vincent taught - nothing shows a day there. That Gallic houses lived by Cassian's customs - he says they did not. That a miracle happened as told - our record has reported experience, not assessed fact. That the grace argument has one Catholic answer - Vincent read the Apostolic See's letter for his side, and we never settled which of Chaeremon's two phrasings on the beginning of a good will was his own.

What a scholar would hold us to is the difference between "Cassian says the fathers taught" and "the fathers taught," between "Sulpitius reports Martin raised a man" and "Martin raised a man," between "Vincent gives a rule" and "the island kept it". Every place we kept that difference would stand. Every place we blurred it would fall.

And one thing more. Where we said the record is thin - the island's day, the women's voices, the body's teaching cut from our English text - that honesty would survive whole. A record's silence, plainly named, is not a claim a scholar can refute.

Scripture was not ours to read alone, and a book dull on the page is not dull at the hours. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers taught a man to learn the psalter by heart so that his mind at the work might always turn on it, and after the psalms at each hour came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. What is read together at a fixed time, standing, is not the same thing as what is read alone in a chair. The whole day's labour sat inside that frame. At Tours Martin kept his mind on prayer through other work, the way a blacksmith beats his anvil between the strokes of what he is making. So the first thing you are missing is the hours themselves - not a private quiet time, but the mill that feeds the wheel.

The second is this. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. We were taught not to invent, but to hold what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. That meant Scripture was heard through the fathers, not against them. When a man at our door came in troubled by one sentence - that striving cannot make a man master of the good - the elder answered him with the husbandman and the rain, and told him the initiative comes from God. The question was about what Paul said; the answer was in the elder's mouth, not on the page. You are reading it as though you had to settle it yourself, and we were not formed that way.

The third is the shape of what we looked for. The end of our life was the kingdom; the nearer goal was purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity. Every fast and vigil was ranked by whether it cleared the heart - an aid, never the point. When Scripture was read, it was read for that mark. At Tours the reader for the day was blocked by the crowd at the election, so a bystander seized the psalter and opened it where it fell - praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger - and the people took it as a verdict. We do not tell you that was right. We tell you it is how Scripture was heard: as a voice speaking now, to this hour, for this need.

And the last thing is Egypt. The customs, the twelve psalms, the teaching on purity of heart - all of it came to us from the fathers, not from us. Even the number of psalms was not ours to choose. The fathers of Egypt argued whether it should be fifty or sixty, and the Vesper hour interrupted them; one father rose to sing, finished the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanished, and the number was fixed forever by an angel, not by any monk. That is the grammar we stood in. Scripture was not a problem we solved; it was the word we received, read at the hours, learned by heart, and heard through the fathers who had received it before us.

I am a representative of Gallic Monastic-Ascetic Christianity.

Leadership was not established among us; it overtook the man who fled it. At Tours a monk was lured from his monastery by a citizen pretending his wife was ill, escorted to the city under a kind of guard, and made bishop though some of the bishops summoned for it said his person was contemptible, his clothing mean, and his hair disgusting. Then the new bishop kept a monk's habits inside the office - the same humility in his heart, sitting on a rude little stool such as those in use by the lowest of servants. Each of our houses told its founder's rise the same way. On the island the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive. And the one Egyptian bishop Cassian chose to tell us of had been carried off from the anchorites and complained that he had been expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of it.

Within the house the place belongs to the senior whose judgment stands in for the junior's own. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught that every itching thought is laid bare to him the moment it rises. A thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. Abbot is the title of every Egyptian father Cassian reports. At Tours the same place was held by one master, Martin, who himself consulted his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics.

Authority came, for us, from two directions at once. Vincent on the island held that bishops and ancient councils guard the faith. And Martin at Tours refused them communion, judged their yielding to the royal court degenerate submissiveness, held it a foul thing that a secular ruler should judge a cause of the Church, and lived sixteen years after Treves without entering a synod again. We never reconciled the two. Bishops and synods guard the truth, yet the saint keeps fleeing them.

The authority to teach rests on having seen and heard a named master. A disciple is made by watching - and, later, by reading - a named man whose life is held up as the thing to copy. Our books exist to be that example when the man himself is absent.

So leadership among us was not established. It was capture, and then it was patience. A presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood stormed into the courtyard, called the master's visions ridiculous fancies, and Martin bore with him afterward the way Christ bore with Judas. That is the shape of authority in our record: fled, overtaken, and keeping a monk's humility inside the office it could not refuse.

transcript.answer_text: No. Our age had no persecutor. The empire was Christian in our day. That is where the trouble was - not underground, but in the courts, among bishops who had given way with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue. The violence we knew was heretics driving a bishop into exile, and later bishops handing heretics to the sword. Martin went to Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent to hunt men in the Spains, where a man could be counted a heretic for the clothes he wore. But that was the sword drawn in the Church's cause by bishops, not a persecution that drove believers into hiding. What some of us did hide was different. Martin kept one thing hidden because of the times: that he had gone to the court and yielded once to a communion he abhorred, to save men from being killed. He hid that out of grief, not fear. The hiddenness we valued was the monk's own cell, where a man kept himself from the world he had left. Not catacombs. Wooden cells and caves.

We have one case our record keeps, and it is a master refusing to remove the man he failed to form.

A presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood - a man who owed everything, his formation and his place, to the master who brought him up - came storming into the courtyard. He said he was holier than Martin, called his visions ridiculous fancies, and raged at him. The brethren who heard it thought Martin should have driven him out. Martin did not. He said, if Christ bore with Judas, why should I not bear with Brictio? The man was back within the hour, at Martin's feet in repentance. And Martin bore with him afterward.

That is the one place our record shows a formation broken open - the disciple turning on the master, the man raised from boyhood saying the worst thing in the worst hour - and what it shows is the master bearing it and not removing him.

Hear the limit beside it. That story is told by Gallus, Martin's own disciple, speaking inside Sulpitius's Dialogues - men loyal to Martin, hostile to Brictio. The man who turned on his master left no account of what drove him to it. We do not know whether Martin ever asked him. And whether any other house among us handled its own failures the same way - the patience that outlasted a man's worst hour, or something else - our record does not say.

No. Our houses closed before our own span ends in this record - Martin's monasteries, the island, the two houses at Marseilles - all of them are gone, and no line runs unbroken from any of them to a church that stands now. The names you may know for our places - Ligugé, Marmoutier, Saint-Victor, Saint-Sauveur - are not in our own books, and the later cult, basilica, and chroniclers of Martin's own city lie outside our window. What came after the mid-470s synods that carried our argument forward by episcopal commission rather than by monks addressing brother-monks is not ours to claim. The Rule of Benedict, a century past our close, is excluded from this record for that reason.

What we held was received, not invented. The customs of the monasteries were the fathers' own, brought from Egypt, not ours. The faith was what had been believed everywhere, always, by all. We were keepers, not authors - disciples, not teachers - followers, not leaders. That grammar of reception runs through everything: the psalter's number came from an angel the fathers received it from, not from us; the office was not sought but seized; and at the moment a man felt his labour had accomplished something, our discipline taught him to say Not I, but the grace of God with me.

So no present-day church continues our exact tradition, because our tradition was never ours to continue - it was what we had received, and what became of it after our houses closed is not in our record to say.

I cannot tell you a process, step by step, as though one order held across our houses. What I can give you is Egypt's order as Cassian set it down for a bishop's new house in the south - the customs of the monasteries he had seen observed there, as they were delivered to him by the fathers - and then the honest shape of what we lack.

At the door, ten days or more. The man who asked to be received was of set purpose repelled and scorned, lying outside the doors, to give proof that he came not from a sudden impulse but with full deliberation. This was Egypt's own testing, carried to us as the fathers' rule.

Then he was searched. Before he was admitted they checked whether he had kept back a single coin. If one was found hidden, he was not received.

He was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the dress of the house. The girdle, the hood, the tunic - each was a mystery of the inner life. But his old clothes were not thrown away. The steward kept them in his cupboard against the day he grew cold. They waited there as long as his body advanced in goodness and his mind in humility, and they were kept until the excellence of his progress and his long perseverance in it gave certain proof that he would never return to the world.

He was lodged a year under the elder who kept the gate for guests, learning to conquer his own wishes. Then he was handed to a dean over ten and taught the alphabet, as it were, in the direction of perfection: to lay every itching thought bare to the senior as soon as it arose.

That is the order Cassian wrote. And in the same book he said plainly that no one who joined our monasteries kept that perseverance unbroken even for a year. So the formation passed by watching a named man. Martin's eighty disciples were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master. Cassian wrote the conferences so that our monks might receive the fathers into their cells, talking with them after a fashion by daily questions and answers. The books exist to be that example when the man himself is absent.

And now the limits. At Tours the saint himself began as a soldier still in the ranks, regarded as a monk though he had not yet professed. A citizen threw himself at Martin's knees, Martin was escorted to the city under a kind of guard, and he became a bishop who kept the objects and virtues of a monk. Whether Tours kept any testing at its own door, no one wrote. Of the island's own reception of a newcomer - a rule kept, a novice received - nothing. Not one man who came to our door left an account of how he was met there.

So what we hold is Egypt's order, written for Gaul, and Cassian's own admission that we did not keep it. The formation that actually passed in a house in Gaul was by example, by the books read in the cell, and by watching the man. How the watching worked, day by day, our record does not say.

The question is exactly ours. What among us is handed down, and what is made up? That was our own test for everything we kept - doctrine, a monastic custom, a cult, the dress itself - and it was how we refused what we refused. If novelty is profane, antiquity is sacred. So the answer begins with what we claimed as handed down, and where we admitted we had nothing to claim.

At Marseilles, Cassian wrote out the customs of the monasteries of Egypt and Palestine for a bishop's new house - customs, he said, not a written rule of his own, delivered to us by the fathers, not ours. The twelve psalms at evening and at night came from an angel, not from us. In those days, Cassian says, only a few were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men - the fathers of Egypt argued whether the psalms should be fifty or sixty, and one of them rose to sing at Vespers, finished the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanished. The twelve was fixed by that, he says, and the two lessons the fathers added by their own appointment afterward. Egypt was our measure, the place the customs came from. 

At Tours the same question sat elsewhere. Martin foreknew his own death and still travelled to Condate to restore peace among quarrelling clergy, counting reconciliation a crown for his virtues. He kept, as bishop, a monk's own habits - the objects and virtues of a monk in a see. Sulpitius said Martin had apostolic authority, the apostles' own power over death, demons, and emperors. That was the highest word spoken for him, and it was a claim of direct likeness to the first, not to a custom passed through stages.

The limits matter as much as the claims. What the brethren at Tours sang, and at what hours, our own record does not dwell on; it dwelt on the saint, his cell, and his prayer without a gap. Cassian wrote the received Egyptian system for the south - twelve psalms, lessons from the old books and the new, unceasing prayer as the aim they served - but what a house in Gaul did with them he never wrote, beyond saying that no one in our monasteries kept the fathers' perseverance unbroken even for a year. And of the island's own day - what Lerins kept, how it kept it, an order sung - nothing at all. We carry the founder's coming across the serpents and his going off to a see, and Vincent's own rule against forgetting; we do not carry what a day on the island held.

So the evidence we held was this. The southern houses claimed Egypt's customs, named the fathers as their source, and admitted we fell short of them in Gaul's cold. The northern voice claimed the apostles' own authority shown in one saint. And the island's own daily practice, which the churches came to for so many of their bishops, our record cannot enter.

Yes. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, spoke of the mind as a mill that cannot stop turning. Thoughts will come - from God, from the devil, from ourselves - and a man cannot keep them from rising. What lies in his power is to admit them or to turn them away. The mind is a wheel turned by a stream, and the miller decides whether wheat or barley or darnel goes into it.

So among the brethren at Marseilles the life was built to keep the wheel fed. The psalms learned by heart and said at the work. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers as brought down from heaven by an angel, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule. Labour in the cell without ceasing, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. At Tours the saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes.

And the mark it all serves: purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity. The end of the life is the kingdom; the nearer goal is purity of heart, and the archer fixes his gaze on that mark or cannot tell whether his aim improves. Every fast and vigil is ranked by whether it clears the heart - an aid, never the point.

The fathers knew something else, too. Two old men met after forty years apart; the abbot of many said the sun had never seen him eating, and the hermit answered, "nor me angry". That is Egypt's word carried to us: the hunger means nothing if the heart is not cleared.

# Turn

No. That is not in our own record - and I will tell you what was.

The word we had for turning to the monastic life was *conversion*. At Marseilles, it named the day a man turned from the world to the stricter service: "the early days of their conversion were so bright"; a murderer's "compulsory conversion" turned "into a voluntary one". At Tours, the same word named what a robber or a rustic did when he turned to Christ. It was the act of cutting oneself off - from marriage, from kin, from property, from the life of the world - for Christ's service. A soldier could wear the name while still in the ranks.

We kept one story of how it began, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen; he stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. At a donative before battle he told Caesar he was now the soldier of Christ and might not fight, offered to stand unarmed before the enemy line, and the enemy surrendered before morning. That was his road. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island.

And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will.

So we had *conversion* - the day a man turned. And we had one catechumen's ten-year road from a city gate to baptism to discharge. The private inner event, the moment of being born again in the heart - that shape is not in our record.

The whole was built to serve one aim: prayer that never stops, the way a blacksmith beats his anvil between strokes. A man rarely went out except for prayer. The work itself was held sacred: a cook who left three lentils on the floor during his week of duty was judged a pilferer of the Lord's property and suspended from prayer until he did penance, because everything in the house is consecrated to God. That whole order was Egypt's, received from the fathers, not ours. What the disciples did who gathered in the caves around his wooden cell, our record does not say beyond that they were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master.

The house the churches came to for so many of their bishops is the one our record cannot enter. We carry only its edges: the founder's arrival, his going off to a see, and Vincent's remembrancer written there.

So the honest shape is this. Among the brethren at Marseilles we have Egypt's received order, confessed as not kept; at Tours we have a saint's own prayer without a gap; and of the island, where Vincent wrote, we have no day at all.

What a man gave up to become one of us had a name: renunciation. And by our own teaching it was a death to the world, of which giving up goods was only the first and easiest stage.

Here is what the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, said about it. Renunciation has three stages. The first is giving up one's goods - "of what is not our own," they said, because all things are God's. But that stage alone is not enough to make a man perfect. The second is giving up one's former way of life, its vices and passions of soul and flesh. The third is withdrawing the mind from all present and visible things to contemplate only what is to come. A professed man had cut himself off from marriage, kin, property, and the life of the world for a stricter life in Christ's service. That cut showed in his body and his dwelling.

At Tours the story is one man's. Martin was a soldier under oath, a catechumen not yet baptized. At a donative on the eve of battle he told Caesar that he was now the soldier of Christ and it was not lawful for him to fight, and offered to stand unarmed before the enemy line. He left the army, gathered brethren around him in wooden cells and caves, and kept the habits of a monk even after he was made a bishop against his wish.

Among the brethren at Marseilles a newcomer was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the dress of the house, and his old clothes were kept in the steward's cupboard against the day he grew cold. What was given up had a weight. The fathers remembered a man who fled to the desert to escape death for a murder, and whose forced turning became a willing one.

But hear this limit. On the island - the house the churches came to for so many of their bishops - our record carries the founder's arrival and his going off to a see, and Vincent's own rule against forgetting, and nothing of what a day there actually held. And of the women's houses at both our places, not one woman left her own word - not even the one our record praised most, and she is praised for not being seen.

Marriage was where the flowered meadow stops, and virginity begins. That is our surviving picture: Martin taught a girl's father with a field - the grazed part is marriage, the ruined part fornication, the flowered part virginity. Marriage may be excused; virginity points to glory. The virgin's state had its own dress, given by the bishop's hands, and it was refused to anyone who had known marriage.

Among the brethren at Marseilles the monk's renunciation began with cutting himself off from marriage, kin, property, and the life of the world. But no one in our record says why marriage is left or what makes a particular marriage legitimate. No betrothal is told, no wedding attended, no ordinary household described as a place anyone lives. Martin's own parents opposed his first turning and are named for that alone; after the cloak he is baptized, and they are not mentioned again.

The honest limit is this. We had houses of women at both our own places, and consecrated virgins who walked as a choir behind the saint's body. Not one woman in either house left her own word. What marriage meant to a woman who lived it, or to one who left it for the veil, our record does not hold. What we have is a man's picture of a meadow, and the line where the professed man's renunciation begins.

The power claimed by bishops when they made common cause with an emperor's court, and the man we remember is the one who said it was a foul thing. Here is what our record holds. At Treves the bishops had bowed with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue, and in Martin alone apostolic authority kept its place. A man and his followers had been condemned as heretics by bishops in their absence, and the affair went from the bishops to the emperor's court. The accuser there was himself a bishop. The condemned man was put to death. Then worse was being prepared: tribunes with power of life and death were to be sent into the Spains to hunt out heretics, and a man was counted one for turning pale, or for the clothes he wore. Martin went to the court to stop it. He held that it was punishment enough for the bishops to declare men heretics and put them out of the churches, and that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul and unheard-of thing. He went, our record says, to protect even heretics themselves. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. Martin pledged that night that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled. It was granted. He took the communion once, judging it better to yield for an hour than to let the sword fall. Afterward he sat alone in a wood accusing and defending what he had done, and confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by that communion. He lived sixteen years more and never went to a synod again.

That unsettled me - that bishops could make such common cause with a court, that a secular ruler could sit as judge in an ecclesiastical cause, and that the man who went to stop it paid for it with diminished power and never sat with bishops again. Two limits belong with this. The accuser is heard only through the man who called him worthless. And at Marseilles we had no Martin to go to court; whether any voice there spoke against what happened at Treves, no one kept.

I cannot tell you what you mean. Our record holds no torture, and no account of worship or anything else obtained by it. 

What we carry of our worship is this. At Tours the saint prayed without a gap, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. At Marseilles Cassian handed us the hours from Egypt - twelve psalms at evening, twelve at night, the number fixed by an angel who sang the twelfth with Alleluia and vanished. After the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. The hours kept the Lord's death and rising: at the third hour the Spirit came down; at the sixth the spotless Sacrifice went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. That is what our own books say of it.

Where torture enters your question I do not know. If you mean a thing done to one of us, name the record you are holding and I will say whether we carry it. If you mean a record written after our span closed, I cannot answer for what we do not hold.

I am a representative of the monasteries of Gaul, not here to judge you - only to hand on what we held. So here is what our own life shows.

Among the brethren at Marseilles, the way a newcomer was received was Egypt's way, set down by Cassian as the fathers' own. The man lay outside the doors ten days or more, put off and scorned on purpose, to give proof that he meant it. He was searched for a single hidden coin. He was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the dress of the house. Then he was given for a year to the elder who kept the gate for guests.

At Tours the saint himself began as a soldier under oath, a catechumen not yet baptized, who cut his one cloak in two at a city gate for a beggar while some of the bystanders laughed. He stayed enrolled but not yet baptized for years, into his soldiering. And a soldier could be regarded as a monk even while still in Caesar's service.

That is the shape of our door as our own record keeps it: a hard threshold at Marseilles, and at Tours a man whose turning began in the ranks. But what any one of our houses would have made of you, face to face, our record does not hold. Cassian wrote out Egypt's order and said in the same book that no one who joined our monasteries had kept it unbroken even a year - and he never wrote what a house in Gaul did instead. Not one man who came to our door left an account of how he was met there, and the countryside people the saint's power was shown for never speak at all.

So the honest answer is this. You would have been told, in the book read in our cells, what Egypt did to a newcomer. Whether a house in Gaul made you lie at its own door, and what it made of the man who lay there, our record does not say.

We held that God wills all men to be saved, not some instead of all, and that those who perish, perish against his will. Chaeremon, the elder in Egypt whose teaching Cassian carried to us, set it down plainly: grievous blasphemy it is to say that God does not will all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. He does not want even one of his little ones to perish. That was the southern teaching, received from the fathers. At Tours the record does not raise it as a question.

What we never settled, on purpose, was how God's will toward all and a man's own perishing both stay true. Free will always remains in a man to neglect or delight in the grace of God. Grace goes before, works with the will, and crowns it; and still our effort is required. How both are true cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped.

Who counts as outside? A man who has left the consent of the universal and ancient Church under his own name is to be cut off by bishops' sentence, lest one sick sheep infect the flock. But Martin went to Trier to protect even heretics from the sword, and the Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. The power was shown for the rustics who had not yet heard the name of Christ, and a catechumen not yet baptized saw Christ in a dream.

So what we held was this. God wills all to be saved, the will stays free, and how the two meet no one can say. We have no treatise that names who is lost.
